comments.author: Alexander Terp
comments.body:
**The method exists: `server.stop`.** This card records that "a `server.shutdown` guess was already tried and refused as an unknown method" - the real spelling is `server.stop`, and it is in `corpus/herdr-0.8.0/api-schema.json` beside `server.reload_config` and `server.live_handoff`. Found while writing `crates/muster-herdr/tests/daemon_isolation.rs`, which uses it to tear its daemon down; it works, and the daemon exits.

So "what close-sessions even means" has an upstream answer to design around rather than a gap. Still worth checking what herdr does to a pane's processes on the way out before promising anything - a clean stop that still SIGKILLs the shells is a different promise from one that does not.

Two other things from today's daemon work that touch this card:

- **`server.live_handoff` is also there**, which sounds like the mechanism behind `herdr update --handoff`. Worth a look for the "quit and leave sessions running" half: if a daemon can hand its session to a successor, that is a better answer than never stopping one.
- **The environment card is closed** (a_28YgGqYq7), and its fix strengthens the case for a lifecycle: the daemon now carries a deliberately chosen environment, which makes a long-lived daemon more defensible - and makes "which daemon am I looking at, and what is it holding" the remaining question. `daemon.starting` and `daemon.environment` in the run log name the socket, the config file and what was scrubbed, which is the beginning of the inventory this card says should be built first.

comments.author: Alexander Terp
comments.body:
**The inventory this card asks for cannot be built from herdr's API
alone**, found by trying to build it by hand today.

You can ask a socket what it holds (`pane.list`, `session.snapshot`), and
you can ask the OS which process holds a socket path (`lsof -p <pid> -U`).
What you cannot do is get from one to the other from the outside: the
schema has `server.stop`, `server.reload_config`, `server.live_handoff`
and `server.agent_manifests`, and nothing that answers "which process are
you". So a person with eight herdr processes cannot pair a pid with the
work it is holding without walking every pid's open sockets and dialing
each path in turn.

Muster is the one thing that already knows the mapping, because it
started the daemon and logged the socket in `daemon.starting`. That
argues the inventory is Muster's to keep rather than herdr's to answer -
a record of the daemons Muster has started, their sockets, and when each
was last attached to, which the run log is already 80% of.

**The hazard is not hypothetical, and it is worse than the card says.**
Today's session, eight herdr processes on this machine: seven were
scratch daemons from agent sessions under `/tmp/m*`, and one - a daemon
started 18 hours earlier, indistinguishable in `ps` from the rest - was
the one holding a working Claude Code in `~/src/nook`. It had been
adopted by a Muster launched today, because it was still answering on
`~/.config/herdr/sessions/muster/herdr.sock` and `daemon::ensure`
attaches to whatever answers. The oldest-looking process was the live
one. Sorting by start time, by binary path, or by "which looks stale"
all point at the wrong process.

What did work, and is the shape the tool should have: for each pid, list
its open unix sockets, dial each `herdr.sock` found, and print what it
holds. That is three lines of shell and it made the decision obvious in
one screen.

comments.author: Alexander Terp
comments.body:
**`server.stop` is a clean stop, measured rather than assumed.** This
card said "worth checking what herdr does to a pane's processes on the
way out before promising anything - a clean stop that still SIGKILLs the
shells is a different promise from one that does not." Answer: it does
not.

Method: a scratch daemon with one pane running `/bin/sh`, with
`trap 'echo HUP >> file' HUP` and the same for TERM installed in the
shell, then `herdr server stop` against that daemon's socket.

Result: the HUP trap fired (twice - the daemon's signal and the PTY
hangup both arrive), the TERM trap did not, and both the shell and the
daemon exited. So a pane's process gets a catchable SIGHUP and a window
to act in, which is the promise a "quit and close sessions" action would
need to be able to make honestly.

What it does not tell us: whether the harnesses people actually run in
these panes handle SIGHUP. Claude Code's behaviour on hangup is the thing
to check before wording any confirmation dialog - "your agents will be
asked to stop" and "your agents will be killed" are different sentences
and only one of them is true, per harness.

Also worth recording for whoever builds the action: as a Muster *user*
there is currently no way to end a daemon at all. The full action list
(`crates/muster-core/src/input/bindings.rs`) has nothing that names a
daemon or a session - `close_pane` is the most destructive thing bound,
and closing every pane leaves the daemon running with an empty window.
The only routes out are a terminal and `pgrep`.

And a sharp edge that argues for building this properly: panes inherit
`HERDR_SESSION=muster`, deliberately, so that `herdr` inside a pane talks
to the daemon that owns it. Which means `herdr server stop` typed in a
Muster pane ends the daemon running the pane it was typed in, along with
every other pane in the window, with no confirmation. That is the one
"kill the session" path a user can reach today, and it is the least
guarded one imaginable.

comments.author: Alexander Terp
comments.body:
Confirmed as wanted, in these words: "something user-friendly for letting
muster users quit while leaving agents working versus quitting and
killing agents." So the two-way choice is the shape to build, and both
halves now have measured answers on this card - leaving them running is
what happens today and costs nothing, and killing them is a catchable
SIGHUP rather than a SIGKILL.

The gap that remains is entirely the user-facing half this card's first
bullet already frames: where the choice lives, and how the destructive
one is guarded.

comments.author: Alexander Terp
comments.body:
**The census this card asks for works, but not by the command the comment above gives.** Measured 2026-08-18, after a day of three agents in parallel worktrees.

`lsof -p <pid> -U` does not filter. lsof ORs its selection options unless told otherwise, so that command returns every unix socket on the machine and each pid appears to hold whichever one grep reaches first. Run over twenty daemons it produced twenty identical rows - the same socket, the same pane, the same cwd - which reads as a finished inventory rather than as a broken one. It needs `lsof -a -p <pid> -U`. Second correction: what lsof shows is `herdr-client.sock`, and the API socket is `herdr.sock` beside it in the same directory, so a census has to derive the path rather than dial what it found.

With both fixed, the answer arrives in one screen exactly as the comment promised:

    20 daemons alive
    19 scratch, sockets under /tmp, panes whose cwd is also under /tmp
     1 real: pid 11093, ~/.config/herdr/herdr.sock, 2d10h old, 2 panes in ~/src

So one process out of twenty held anybody's work, and it was the homebrew herdr rather than any Muster started. Sorting by age would have picked the wrong one again: the real daemon was neither the oldest (2d13h) nor the youngest.

**None came from that day's three agents.** The youngest was 18 hours old and the oldest 2.5 days; every one traced to a smoke-launch fixture (/tmp/muster-smoke/...), a harness daemon (/tmp/muster-test/<pid>-0/), or an ad-hoc scratch dir (/tmp/hh, /tmp/mt, /tmp/msl, /tmp/mhy, /tmp/mhz). The test harness does tear its own down. What accumulates is what a person or a fixture started outside it.

**They are not why a gate is slow, and that is worth stating.** Twenty of them together drew 0.1% CPU. A full `./dev` on the same machine took 12m35s warm-cache with them all running, against the 27.1 and 43.8 minutes recorded on a_29iw10a58. So this card's case is safety and legibility - knowing which process holds work before killing it - and not performance. Anybody reaching for a_29iw10a58's 'stray processes' framing to justify a lifecycle here would be arguing from a cost that does not exist.

Measured while chasing what looked like a slow gate and was neither the machine nor the daemons: the harness running `./dev` capped background commands at ten minutes and killed two runs mid-suite. Ruling out load, memory and these daemons is how the census got taken.

creator: Alexander Terp
description:
There is no lifecycle at all today. `daemon.rs` says "Started, never stopped" and puts the daemon in its own process group so quitting Muster cannot touch it; the shell's only quit handling is `applicationShouldTerminateAfterLastWindowClosed: true`. So the daemon leaks forward forever, and the only way to end one is to find it with `pgrep` and kill it - which also destroys whatever is running in its panes, as happened once already this week.

**The default is right and should stay.** Sessions outliving the app is a founding desideratum: quit Muster, come back, and every pane is where you left it. Nothing here proposes changing that.

What is missing is that it is the *only* behaviour, and it is invisible. Somebody who is finished for the day has no way to say so. Somebody who has accumulated daemons from a week of launches has no way to know, and no way to tidy up that does not risk killing live work.

Worth deciding rather than defaulting:

- **What quit offers, and where.** A menu item ("Quit and leave sessions running" beside "Quit and close sessions") is discoverable; a modifier on ⌘Q is not. Consider that the destructive one is the one that needs confirming, and that a person with three agents mid-task must not be able to end them by reflex.
- **What "close sessions" even means.** Ending the daemon kills processes that have no way to save; ending it *cleanly* means asking herdr, which may or may not have an answer worth relying on. Check what herdr offers before designing around it - a `server.shutdown` guess was already tried and refused as an unknown method.
- **How you find out what is still running.** Nothing today lists Muster's daemons or what they hold. That is the piece that makes tidying up safe rather than a `pgrep` gamble, and it is probably the first half to build.
- **Whether a daemon nobody has attached to in weeks should say so**, rather than being reaped automatically. Automatic reaping of a process holding somebody's work is the wrong default in a tool built on the promise that it will not.

Related: the isolation card - a daemon that outlives the app is exactly why the environment it was started with matters so much.
title: 🔌 Quitting Muster should decide what happens to its daemons
